In brief

After the young men "Scrum in" to the pub, someone asks who's going to pay for drinks, and a lot of poverty is pled: "Query. Who's astanding this here do? Proud possessor of damnall. Declare misery. Bet to the ropes. Me nantee saltee. Not a red at me this week gone." At last someone steps up and starts taking orders. He begins with Mulligan, and then others second Mulligan's choice of a Number One Bass Ale: "Yours? Mead of our fathers for the Uebermensch. Dittoh. Five number ones." The person who takes the initiative seems to be Stephen Dedalus, since he listened to Mulligan styling himself a Nietzschean superman in Telemachus.

At more length

In a widespread English idiom, to "stand" means to pay for a round of drinks, and standing rounds is a time-honored Irish custom. But one man after another pleads poverty. One says ironically that he's the "Proud possessor of damnall"—i.e., no money at all. Another simply declares "misery." A third one—probably Lenehan, who has been loudly bemoaning Sceptre's performance in the Gold Cup—says he has "Bet to the ropes," perhaps drawing on boxing terminology to suggest that his racetrack losses have him on the ropes. Another person, drawing on the ancient association between money and salt, says, in pidgin English, "Me nantee saltee." Roman soldiers were paid in salt, hence "salary," and many expressions like "not worth one's salt" and "salting away" money perpetuate the ancient metaphor. A fifth man says that for all the last week he has had "Not a red." The expression "Not a red cent," meaning "flat broke," originated in America, where pennies, the smallest unit of currency, were minted from copper.

Stephen was the one who suggested that the group leave the hospital and head down to "Burke's!," just as he suggested in Aeolus that a different group (Lenehan, fittingly, is a hanger-on in both) leave the newspaper offices and head for a pub: "As the next motion on the agenda paper may I suggest that the house do now adjourn?" In both cases, like the proverbial drunken sailor he extravagantly throws away his month's wages on drinks with people who mean little to him. The noontime binge in Mooney's gave him an occasion to frustrate Mulligan's declaration in Telemachus that "We'll have a glorious drunk" at Stephen's expense at The Ship, but now he turns first to that self-proclaimed superman.

One more strange quirk may lurk in this exchange. Samuel Keays suggests in a personal communication that "Me nantee saltee" shows Stephen Dedalus echoing Italian—"mi nenti soldi," I have no money—while continuing to mull the Dantean trope heard in Telemachus of eating another's salt bread. This ingenious reading coheres with Stephen's condition of wretched poverty and his resentment of having to rely on Mulligan for room and board. It is harder to reconcile with the fact that on this particular day Stephen has plenty of money in his pocket and dispenses it with prodigal liberality, including in this very bar. Is it conceivable that he would say he has no money shortly before paying for everyone's drinks? Possibly so, because two paragraphs later people observe that the bartender has not yet been paid and remind Stephen that coming to the pub was his idea: "Us come right in on your invite, see? Up to you, matey. Out with the oof."

John Hunt 2026
